Then, one evening, my little brother's kite blew out over the lagoon, and before I could think, I had waded in up to my knees to grab the string. The water was warm. That surprised me so much that I just stood there, holding the kite, while tiny silver fish nibbled at my ankles as if they were checking whether I was edible. A turtle surfaced a few metres away, looked at me with its old, wrinkled face and sank again without a sound. I stayed until the sun went down. I still think the sea tastes like a pickled sock. But now, every evening, I am the first one in the water, and Mum has to drag me out when it gets dark.

The only sound was the hum of the air conditioning. One engineer chewed his pen until it cracked. The flight director, a tall woman named Dr Ferris, stood perfectly still with her arms folded and her eyes fixed on the clock. At 9.02 pm, the dot reappeared, and a voice burst through the speakers, half laughing: 'Control, Selene 4. We're coming home, and we've brought you a rock shaped like a potato.' The room exploded into cheers. Mum hugged me so hard that my badge fell off. Dr Ferris told the gallery that the crew were safe and would splash down in three days. To this day, though, the astronauts have never said what they were laughing about when the radio came back on.

She walked to the edge of a river and found that the water didn't splash; it just shimmered, like a picture of water. A sign beside the path said SAVE POINT, and when she touched it, a cheerful chime rang out from nowhere. Further along, a frog hopped past her, stopped, hopped back the other way, and then did exactly the same thing again, over and over, as if it had forgotten how to do anything else. When she finally tripped over a root and fell into the river, everything went black. A moment later, she was standing beside the SAVE POINT sign again, completely dry, with her green bar full. High above the trees, in the top corner of the sky, a small white message flickered: PLAYER 2 HAS JOINED. Kestrel looked up and narrowed her eyes. Somewhere, she realised, someone was holding a controller, and she had a very good idea who it was.

text: Every autumn, the shearwater chicks of Twotide Atoll leave their burrows and fly north, thousands of kilometres across open ocean, without a single adult to show them the way. The other chicks had left weeks earlier, and his parents had gone too, as shearwater parents always do, so the burrow grew colder and Kip grew hungrier. Then, one evening, a storm rolled in, and the waves began to eat away at the dune, metre by metre, until the sea was lapping at the mouth of his burrow. He scrambled to the top of the last patch of sand, shut his eyes and jumped into the wind. He didn't fly well. He wobbled, dipped and nearly clipped a wave. But he flew. By the time the sun came up, the island was a speck behind him, and Kip was no longer afraid of the sky. He was far too busy looking for breakfast.

text: Captain Lulu Snodgrass had been in charge of the starship Crumpet for exactly four minutes when the first thing went wrong. (It was a new record. The old record was six minutes, and that was also Lulu.) Outside the window, the planet Zorb hung in space, a vast swirl of violet and emerald clouds that rolled slowly across its surface like paint stirred into a tin of cream. It was, everyone agreed, the most beautiful planet in the galaxy. It was also the smelliest. Nobody had told Lulu that part. As the Crumpet drifted closer, the stink seeped in through the air vents, a thick, eggy, cabbagey, sock-drawer sort of smell that made the ship's cat faint dramatically onto the control panel. (The cat was fine. The control panel was not.) Lights flashed. Alarms howled. The Crumpet began to spin. 'Do something!' shouted the first officer, a nervous robot called Kevin who was mostly made of old toasters. Lulu did something. She opened a window. (Never open a window in space. I cannot stress this enough. Write it on your hand.) Luckily, the Crumpet's windows had been installed upside down, so instead of everybody being sucked out into space, the stink was sucked out instead. Lulu was awarded a medal for quick thinking. She accepted it with great dignity, then tripped over the cat on her way off the stage.

text: Factory Nine. Midnight. The machines were silent. Rain hammered the tin roof. Juno slipped through the gate. Torch off. Breath held. She had one job: find the missing drone and get out before the guards came back. Ten minutes. No more. The guards' hut was dark. Empty. A cup of tea sat on the desk. Juno touched it. Still warm. Someone had been here. Recently. She crept along the wall. Puddles. Wire. Broken glass. Then a hum. Low. Electric. Juno froze. The hum was coming from the main hall. She pushed the door. It creaked. She waited. Counted to ten. Nothing came. She slipped inside. A green glow came from somewhere. Up ahead. Rows of robots stood in the dark, frozen mid-step. Hundreds of them. Waiting. Juno crept between the rows. Left. Right. Left. Each robot was taller than her. Each one had its head bowed. Metal hands. Fingers curled. Ready. Her shoes squeaked on the wet floor. She stopped. Listened. Nothing. She took another step. Click. A red eye blinked open. Then another. Then all of them.

text: Midnight. The harbour was still. Too still. Detective Rook stood on the jetty. Waiting. Watching. The fog rolled in. Thick. Grey. Like porridge, but less tasty. Somewhere, a boat creaked. His coat was wet. His shoes were wet. Even his sandwich was wet. Soggy. Like his career. Rook ate it anyway. Detectives can't be fussy. He checked his watch. Five past twelve. The smuggler was late. Smugglers were always late. It was the one thing you could count on, apart from their terrible fashion sense. A sound. Footsteps. Rook spun around. Nothing. Just a seagull. It glared at him. He glared back. The seagull won. Then a light flickered out on the water. Once. Twice. Three times. The signal. Rook crouched behind a stack of crates. Clang. A boat bumped the jetty. A figure climbed out. Tall. Thin. Carrying a box. A moustache. Fake. Badly glued. Rook's heart pounded. This was it. Six months of work. He jumped out. 'Freeze!' The figure froze. The box fell. It burst open on the jetty. Fish fingers. Hundreds of them. Rook stared. The smuggler stared. 'They're for my nan,' said the smuggler. Rook sighed. It was going to be a long night. Then, behind them both, the water began to bubble.

text:
Extract A. You have played this game before, haven't you? You know the level with the broken bridge. You know the music that plays when the lights go out. But have you ever noticed the door at the end of the hall? You walk past it every time. Tonight, try the handle. You will find it isn't locked. You will find a room you have never seen, with a single controller on the floor. The screen flickers, but you keep playing. Your thumbs feel cold. Somewhere in your house, a door you didn't open swings shut. Don't turn around. Not yet. First, look at the controller on the floor of that room. Look closely. It is the same colour as yours. It has the same scratch on the left button. It is yours.

Extract B. You've played Robo Brawl, right? (If not, where have you BEEN?) You know the bit where the giant toaster attacks? I have lost to that toaster four hundred times. (It's a very good toaster.) So here's my tip: hide behind the fridge. The toaster hates fridges. Nobody knows why. (Possibly a family thing.) Also, never trust the kettle on level six. It looks friendly. It is not friendly. (It once stole my lunch. I'm still upset.) If you beat the toaster, you win a golden crumpet. I have never seen the golden crumpet. My cousin says it's real. My cousin also says he once ate a whole watermelon in one bite, so.
